title: A level Paper 1 mock — Set B: Markets and business behaviour
description: A full two-hour A level Paper 1 mock covering Theme 1 (consumer behaviour, elasticity, externalities and government failure) and Theme 3 (revenue and costs, market structures, contestability and regulation). Section A has five multiple-choice and five short-answer questions worth 25 marks: aim for about 25 minutes, showing working in all calculations. Section B is a 50-mark data response on local bus services in a fictional city region: allow around 60 minutes, read the tables and all three extracts before starting, and use calculations from the data in your analysis. Section C offers a choice of two 25-mark essays: allow about 35 minutes, plan both sides of the argument and finish with a justified judgement.

questions.prompt: A restaurant places a £120 bottle of wine at the top of its wine list, although it rarely sells one. Sales of the £40 bottles listed beneath it increase. Which concept best explains the change in customer behaviour?
options: A Altruism
B Rational choice based on perfect information
C Anchoring
D Habitual behaviour
questions.explanation: Anchoring is a cognitive bias in which people rely heavily on the first piece of information they see as a reference point. The £120 price acts as an anchor, so £40 appears good value by comparison, even though nothing about the £40 wine has changed. This contradicts the traditional model of rational choice (B). Altruism (A) concerns concern for others, and habit (D) would not explain a change in purchases.

questions.prompt: A consumer spends all of her weekly budget on coffees costing £3 each and sandwiches costing £5 each. For the last coffee she buys, her marginal utility is 30 units; for the last sandwich it is 40 units. To maximise her total utility with the same budget she should
options: A buy more sandwiches and fewer coffees.
B buy more coffees and fewer sandwiches.
C make no change, because she is already maximising utility.
D buy fewer of both goods.
questions.explanation: Utility is maximised when marginal utility per pound is equal across goods (MU of coffee ÷ price of coffee = MU of sandwiches ÷ price of sandwiches). Coffee gives 30 ÷ 3 = 10 units per £1; sandwiches give 40 ÷ 5 = 8 units per £1. Switching spending from sandwiches to coffee raises total utility; as she buys more coffee its marginal utility diminishes, and the ratios move towards equality. A wrongly compares total MU without dividing by price; D would leave income unspent.

questions.prompt: A firm faces a straight-line, downward-sloping demand (average revenue) curve. At the output at which its marginal revenue is zero,
options: A total revenue is maximised and price elasticity of demand is equal to −1.
B profit is maximised.
C demand is price elastic, so a price cut would raise total revenue.
D average revenue is also zero.
questions.explanation: When MR is zero, selling one more unit adds nothing to total revenue, so TR is at its maximum. On a linear demand curve this occurs at the midpoint, where PED is unitary (−1). Above that point demand is elastic and MR is positive; below it demand is inelastic and MR is negative, so C is wrong. Profit is maximised where MC = MR, which is at zero MR only if MC is zero (B). AR is positive at this output (D).

questions.prompt: A hospital trust is the only major employer of nurses in a town. It employs 10 nurses at £600 per week each. To recruit an eleventh nurse it must raise the weekly wage to £620 for all its nurses. What is the marginal cost of labour of the eleventh nurse?
questions.explanation: Total labour cost rises from 10 × £600 = £6,000 to 11 × £620 = £6,820, so the marginal cost of labour is £6,820 − £6,000 = £820. This is above the wage of £620 (the average cost of labour) because the monopsonist must pay the higher wage to all existing nurses as well. This is why a monopsony employs fewer workers at a lower wage than a competitive market. B is the new wage (ACL), C is total cost and A is only the wage increase per worker.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would most likely cause a rightward shift of the supply curve of labour to the nursing profession?
options: A A rise in the wage rate paid to nurses
B A fall in the demand for hospital treatment
C An improvement in working conditions, including more flexible shift patterns
D An increase in the length of training needed to qualify as a nurse
questions.explanation: Non-wage factors such as working conditions, flexibility and job satisfaction shift the labour supply curve: at every wage more people are willing to work as nurses. A rise in the wage (A) causes a movement along the supply curve, not a shift. B affects the demand for labour, not supply. D raises the cost of entering the profession and would shift supply to the left.

questions.prompt: With the help of a production possibility frontier diagram, explain the opportunity cost to an economy at full employment of increasing its production of capital goods, and one long-run benefit of doing so.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points (4 marks):
1 mark: definition of opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative forgone.
1 mark: correctly labelled PPF diagram (capital goods on one axis, consumer goods on the other) showing a movement along the frontier from one point to another, with more capital goods and fewer consumer goods.
1 mark: explanation that, at full employment, resources must be reallocated from producing consumer goods, so the opportunity cost is the consumer goods forgone (lower current consumption and living standards).
1 mark: long-run benefit: the larger capital stock increases productive capacity, shifting the PPF outwards in future, allowing more of both goods (economic growth / higher future living standards).
A diagram showing a shift without a movement along the PPF scores only the long-run benefit mark for the diagram content.

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why an indirect tax imposed to correct a negative externality may result in government failure.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points (4 marks): for each of two reasons, 1 mark for identification and 1 mark for a linked explanation of why it leads to a net welfare loss or a worse allocation of resources.
Possible reasons:
- Information gaps: the government cannot measure the marginal external cost accurately, so the tax may be set too high (under-production) or too low (over-production remains).
- Price inelastic demand: if demand is inelastic, quantity falls little, so the externality is barely reduced while consumers bear most of the tax.
- Unintended consequences: higher prices encourage smuggling, cross-border shopping or illegal markets, which can increase harm and reduce tax revenue.
- Distortion of price signals / regressive effects: the tax may hit low-income households hardest, worsening equity.
- Administrative and compliance costs that exceed the welfare gain.
- Political influence or lobbying leading to a tax set for revenue rather than efficiency.
No marks for describing market failure without linking it to the tax.

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why many small firms continue to survive in markets dominated by large firms.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points (4 marks): for each of two reasons, 1 mark for identification and 1 mark for a developed explanation.
Possible reasons:
- Niche markets and product differentiation: small firms serve specialised demand that large firms find unprofitable, so they face less direct competition.
- Limited extent of the market: local services (hairdressers, plumbers) have demand too small or dispersed for large firms to exploit economies of scale.
- Low minimum efficient scale: where economies of scale are exhausted at low output, small firms can produce at a similar average cost to large ones.
- Flexibility and personal service: small firms can respond quickly to customers and build loyalty, avoiding diseconomies of scale.
- Owners' objectives: owners may satisfice or value independence, accepting lower profit than a large firm would require.
- Government support or subcontracting for large firms.
One mark maximum for a reason that is stated without explanation.

questions.prompt: Using a diagram, explain why a firm in a perfectly competitive market earns only normal profit in the long run.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points (4 marks):
1 mark: accurate diagram(s): industry supply and demand setting price; firm's horizontal AR = MR = P line with MC cutting AC at its minimum, and the long-run equilibrium where P = MR = MC = minimum AC.
1 mark: in the short run, supernormal profit (AR above AC at the output where MC = MR) acts as a signal to other firms.
1 mark: because there are no barriers to entry and there is perfect information, new firms enter, shifting industry supply to the right and lowering the market price.
1 mark: entry continues until price falls to the minimum of AC, where AR = AC and only normal profit is earned (the reverse process applies to losses, with firms leaving).
Accept a correct explanation of the exit process from a short-run loss as an alternative to entry.

questions.prompt: Explain, using the kinked demand curve model, why prices may be stable in an oligopolistic market.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points (4 marks):
1 mark: the key assumption: rivals will match a price cut (to avoid losing market share) but will not follow a price rise (to gain customers).
1 mark: above the current price, demand is price elastic, so a firm that raises its price loses many customers and total revenue falls.
1 mark: below the current price, demand is price inelastic because rivals match the cut, so a price cut lowers total revenue.
1 mark: the kink creates a vertical discontinuity in the MR curve, so marginal cost can change within that gap without changing the profit-maximising price and output (MC = MR); so the firm has little incentive to change price.
A correctly labelled diagram can earn the third and fourth marks where the explanation is clear from it.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate the price elasticity of demand for bus journeys in Kestermoor between 2023 and 2024. Explain one reason why this figure should be interpreted with caution.
questions.context:
Local bus services in Kestermoor (illustrative data)

Kestermoor is a fictional city region in England with a population of around 1.2 million.

Table 1: The Kestermoor bus market, 2015–2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Average adult single fare (£) | Passenger journeys (millions) | Bus distance operated (million vehicle-km) | Number of operators
2015 | 2.40 | 92 | 41 | 9
2019 | 2.90 | 84 | 38 | 6
2023 | 3.20 | 66 | 33 | 4
2024 | 2.00 | 75 | 33 | 4
2025 | 2.00 | 79 | 34 | 4

Table 2: Ridgeway Buses, revenue and costs by type of route, 2025 (£ per vehicle-km, illustrative data)
Route type | Average revenue (including fare-cap compensation) | Average variable cost | Average total cost
Inter-urban corridors | 4.10 | 2.30 | 3.20
Suburban | 3.10 | 2.40 | 3.30
Rural | 2.60 | 2.50 | 3.60

Extract A: A deregulated market
Outside London, local bus services in England have been deregulated since 1986: any licensed operator can run a commercial route after registering it, and set its own fares and timetables. In Kestermoor the number of operators has fallen from nine to four since 2015. Ridgeway Buses now runs around two-thirds of all services and owns the two largest depots in the city, and other operators say suitable depot sites are very hard to find. A new electric double-deck bus costs several hundred thousand pounds, although buses can be leased and can be resold or moved to other areas. Ridgeway's day tickets are not valid on other operators' buses, so passengers who need to change buses tend to use Ridgeway for their whole journey.

In 2022 a small operator, Lark Coaches, started running on Ridgeway's busiest corridor. Ridgeway added extra buses timed to arrive a few minutes before Lark's and cut fares on that corridor only. Lark withdrew after eight months, and Ridgeway's fares on the corridor then returned to their previous level. Ridgeway says it was simply responding to competition. All operators also report a shortage of qualified drivers: training a new driver takes several weeks and costs the operator several thousand pounds.

Extract B: The fare cap and the case for subsidy
In January 2024 the Kestermoor Combined Authority introduced a £2 cap on adult single fares, compensating operators for lost revenue. The cap costs around £18 million a year. Supporters point out that around a quarter of households in Kestermoor do not have a car, that buses reduce congestion and vehicle emissions on the city's main roads, and that cheaper travel helps people on low incomes reach jobs, education and health appointments. Older and disabled people already travel free under the national concessionary pass scheme.

Critics argue that much of the money goes to people who would have travelled by bus anyway, and that surveys show passengers value frequency and reliability more highly than lower fares. They say the £18 million would be better spent restoring routes that have been cut, especially in suburban and rural areas, where Ridgeway has warned that some services may be withdrawn.

Extract C: Franchising
The Combined Authority is consulting on bus franchising, a model already introduced in Greater Manchester. Under franchising, the authority would decide routes, timetables and fares, and would keep the fare revenue. Operators would bid in competitive tenders for contracts, typically lasting five to seven years, to run groups of routes, and would be paid a fee per vehicle-km operated, with bonuses or penalties linked to punctuality. The authority would buy the main depots so that any winning bidder could use them, and a single ticket would be valid on all buses.

Supporters say franchising would create an integrated network, allow profitable corridors to cross-subsidise socially valuable routes, and replace competition on the road with competition for the market. Critics point out that the authority would bear the risk if passenger numbers fall, that the transition is estimated to cost tens of millions of pounds, and that Ridgeway may be the only operator large enough to bid for most contracts.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points (5 marks):
1 mark: % change in quantity demanded = (75 − 66) ÷ 66 × 100 = +13.6%.
1 mark: % change in price = (2.00 − 3.20) ÷ 3.20 × 100 = −37.5%.
1 mark: PED = 13.6 ÷ −37.5 = −0.36 (accept −0.36 or −0.37), which shows that demand is price inelastic.
Up to 2 marks for one reason for caution, explained (1 for the reason, 1 for development), e.g.:
- Ceteris paribus is unlikely to hold: passenger numbers may have been recovering anyway (journeys were falling sharply before 2023), so not all of the rise is due to the fare cap.
- The average fare covers only adult single fares, while many journeys use season tickets, day tickets or free concessionary passes, so the price change faced by many passengers was smaller.
- One year is the short run: demand may become more elastic as people change commuting habits or give up a car (journeys rose further in 2025 at an unchanged fare).
- Service levels (vehicle-km) were unchanged, but reliability or frequency may have changed, affecting demand.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge/Application: Contestable market: one where entry and exit are easy and costless, so the threat of entry forces incumbents to keep prices close to average cost. Barriers to entry: structural (sunk costs, control of essential facilities, economies of scale, network effects) and strategic (predatory pricing, limit pricing, capacity flooding). Application: Ridgeway runs about two-thirds of services; owns the two largest depots; day tickets not valid on rival buses; Lark Coaches withdrew after eight months; operators fell from nine to four (Table 1); driver training costs several thousand pounds.
Analysis: Barrier 1, control of depots: an entrant needs a nearby depot to store, charge and maintain buses; if sites are unavailable it faces higher costs (longer empty running) or cannot enter, so Ridgeway can price above average cost without attracting entry. Barrier 2, strategic behaviour: Ridgeway's response to Lark (extra buses timed just ahead and corridor-specific fare cuts, reversed after Lark left) is consistent with predatory pricing; potential entrants expect losses, so the threat of entry no longer disciplines prices. Barrier 3, network effects from ticketing: passengers who change buses prefer a single operator's day ticket, so an entrant on one route cannot attract them even with a lower fare. Sunk costs: driver training, marketing and registration costs cannot be recovered on exit, raising the risk of entry. Higher barriers mean the market is less contestable, so the incumbent can earn supernormal profit and may be X-inefficient.
Evaluation: Some apparent barriers are weak: buses can be leased, resold or moved, so the largest capital cost is not sunk, which is why bus markets were once thought highly contestable. The effect of predation depends on whether it is credible and whether competition authorities intervene (abuse of a dominant position is illegal). The fall from nine to four operators may also reflect falling demand (journeys down from 92 to 66 million by 2023), not only barriers. Which barrier matters most: depot control and ticketing are permanent, while predation is occasional.
Levels: Knowledge, application and analysis (up to 6 marks)
Level 1 (1–2): Isolated knowledge, often limited to definitions; little or no use of the extracts or data; analysis is absent or a list of unconnected assertions.
Level 2 (3–4): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but are incomplete or one-sided; any diagram is partly accurate or not explained.
Level 3 (5–6): Precise knowledge fully integrated with the extracts and figures; developed, logical chains of reasoning for each point; accurate diagrams (where relevant) explained and used in the argument.
Levels: Evaluation (up to 2 marks)
Level 1 (1): Generic or unsupported evaluative comment.
Level 2 (2): Evaluative comment that is supported by reasoning or by reference to the data, e.g. weighing the relative importance of the two points.
A* answer: Explains two barriers with full chains linking each to reduced contestability and higher prices or lower efficiency, uses the Lark example and Table 1, and judges which barrier is most significant, recognising that bus capital is mobile.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge/Application: Positive externality: a benefit to third parties not reflected in the price; marginal social benefit (MSB) exceeds marginal private benefit (MPB), so the free market under-consumes and there is a welfare loss. A subsidy lowers the price consumers pay. Application: a quarter of households have no car; reduced congestion and emissions; access to jobs, education and health care; cap costs around £18 million a year; journeys rose from 66 million to 75 million in 2024 and 79 million in 2025.
Analysis: Diagram: MPB below MSB; market equilibrium where MPB = MSC at Q1 is below the social optimum Q*; welfare loss triangle. A subsidy shifts supply (MPC) down, or lowers the price passengers pay, increasing journeys towards Q* and removing the welfare loss. Each car journey replaced by a bus journey reduces congestion for other road users (time savings, lower business costs) and cuts emissions, improving air quality and public health. Better access to jobs for car-less low-income households increases employment and output, with wider benefits to the regional economy and tax revenues. There is also an equity argument, as bus users have lower average incomes.
Evaluation: PED of about −0.36 (Table 1) means the subsidy produced a relatively small rise in journeys for its cost: much of the £18 million is a transfer to passengers who would have travelled anyway, so the welfare gain per pound may be low. The externalities only arise if new bus journeys replace car journeys rather than walking or cycling. The size of the external benefit is hard to estimate (information gaps causing government failure). Passengers value frequency and reliability more than fares, so subsidising routes may generate more benefit than subsidising fares. Opportunity cost of the funds. Over time, a sustained low fare may change habits and car ownership, increasing the effect.
Levels: Knowledge, application and analysis (up to 6 marks)
Level 1 (1–2): Isolated knowledge, often limited to definitions; little or no use of the extracts or data; analysis is absent or a list of unconnected assertions.
Level 2 (3–4): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but are incomplete or one-sided; any diagram is partly accurate or not explained.
Level 3 (5–6): Precise knowledge fully integrated with the extracts and figures; developed, logical chains of reasoning for each point; accurate diagrams (where relevant) explained and used in the argument.
Levels: Evaluation (up to 4 marks)
Level 1 (1–2): Evaluation is generic or asserted, with little reference to the context or data; no clear judgement.
Level 2 (3–4): Evaluation is supported by the data and reasoning, considers alternative outcomes or relative significance, and reaches a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Draws an accurate MSB/MPB diagram showing the subsidy moving output to the social optimum, applies specific external benefits from Extract B, and uses the PED from Table 1 to weigh the size of the benefit against the cost and the alternative use of the subsidy.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge/Application: Short-run shutdown point: a firm should continue to produce as long as average revenue covers average variable cost (AR ≥ AVC). Long-run shutdown point: a firm should leave the market if AR is below average total cost (AR < ATC), since it cannot earn normal profit. Normal profit includes the opportunity cost of capital. Application: suburban AR £3.10, AVC £2.40, ATC £3.30; rural AR £2.60, AVC £2.50, ATC £3.60; inter-urban AR £4.10, ATC £3.20; revenue includes fare-cap compensation.
Analysis: Suburban routes: AR exceeds AVC by £0.70 per vehicle-km, contributing towards fixed costs, but are £0.20 below ATC, so they make a loss. In the short run the loss of £0.20 per km is smaller than the £0.90 of fixed cost per km that would still have to be paid if the service stopped, so they should continue. Rural routes: AR (£2.60) only just exceeds AVC (£2.50), contributing £0.10 per km, with a loss of £1.00 per km; in the short run continuing still reduces losses, but the margin is very narrow. In the long run, unless revenue rises or costs fall, both route types should be withdrawn, as fixed costs become variable and resources could earn more elsewhere. Inter-urban routes make a profit of £0.90 per km and can cross-subsidise losses. Wider considerations: suburban and rural routes may feed passengers onto profitable inter-urban corridors (network effects), so the true revenue contribution is understated.
Evaluation: The rural margin of £0.10 is fragile: a small rise in driver wages (the driver shortage) or fuel costs would push AVC above AR, so Ridgeway should shut down immediately. Revenue includes fare-cap compensation, which may be withdrawn, cutting AR. The split between fixed and variable cost is uncertain: depots and buses can be redeployed, so some 'fixed' costs are avoidable and the true AVC is higher. Objectives: a private firm aiming to maximise profit would withdraw in the long run; a firm that satisfices or values its reputation and relationship with the authority (especially ahead of franchising) may continue. If Ridgeway withdraws, the authority may need to tender and subsidise the routes, or franchising would make the decision irrelevant. Exit could also invite a rival to enter the suburban routes.
Levels: Knowledge, application and analysis (up to 8 marks)
Level 1 (1–2): Isolated knowledge, often limited to definitions; little or no use of the extracts or data; analysis is absent or descriptive.
Level 2 (3–4): Accurate knowledge with some application to the context; chains of reasoning are partial or one-sided; limited use of the figures; diagrams may contain errors.
Level 3 (5–6): Accurate knowledge applied to the context using relevant figures; several developed chains of reasoning, with minor gaps; diagrams mostly accurate and explained.
Level 4 (7–8): Precise, relevant knowledge applied throughout, with data manipulated (not just quoted); fully developed, logical chains of reasoning; accurate diagrams integrated into the analysis.
Levels: Evaluation (up to 4 marks)
Level 1 (1–2): Evaluation is generic or asserted, with little reference to the context or data; no clear judgement.
Level 2 (3–4): Evaluation is supported by the data and reasoning, considers alternative outcomes or relative significance, and reaches a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Calculates the per-km contribution and loss for each route type, applies the short-run and long-run shutdown rules correctly, recognises network effects and cross-subsidy, and makes a differentiated judgement (for example, keep suburban routes in the short run but review rural routes, depending on compensation and wage costs).

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether franchising, as described in Extract C, is likely to improve outcomes for bus passengers in Kestermoor compared with the current deregulated market.
questions.context:
Local bus services in Kestermoor (illustrative data)

Kestermoor is a fictional city region in England with a population of around 1.2 million.

Table 1: The Kestermoor bus market, 2015–2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Average adult single fare (£) | Passenger journeys (millions) | Bus distance operated (million vehicle-km) | Number of operators
2015 | 2.40 | 92 | 41 | 9
2019 | 2.90 | 84 | 38 | 6
2023 | 3.20 | 66 | 33 | 4
2024 | 2.00 | 75 | 33 | 4
2025 | 2.00 | 79 | 34 | 4

Table 2: Ridgeway Buses, revenue and costs by type of route, 2025 (£ per vehicle-km, illustrative data)
Route type | Average revenue (including fare-cap compensation) | Average variable cost | Average total cost
Inter-urban corridors | 4.10 | 2.30 | 3.20
Suburban | 3.10 | 2.40 | 3.30
Rural | 2.60 | 2.50 | 3.60

Extract A: A deregulated market
Outside London, local bus services in England have been deregulated since 1986: any licensed operator can run a commercial route after registering it, and set its own fares and timetables. In Kestermoor the number of operators has fallen from nine to four since 2015. Ridgeway Buses now runs around two-thirds of all services and owns the two largest depots in the city, and other operators say suitable depot sites are very hard to find. A new electric double-deck bus costs several hundred thousand pounds, although buses can be leased and can be resold or moved to other areas. Ridgeway's day tickets are not valid on other operators' buses, so passengers who need to change buses tend to use Ridgeway for their whole journey.

In 2022 a small operator, Lark Coaches, started running on Ridgeway's busiest corridor. Ridgeway added extra buses timed to arrive a few minutes before Lark's and cut fares on that corridor only. Lark withdrew after eight months, and Ridgeway's fares on the corridor then returned to their previous level. Ridgeway says it was simply responding to competition. All operators also report a shortage of qualified drivers: training a new driver takes several weeks and costs the operator several thousand pounds.

Extract B: The fare cap and the case for subsidy
In January 2024 the Kestermoor Combined Authority introduced a £2 cap on adult single fares, compensating operators for lost revenue. The cap costs around £18 million a year. Supporters point out that around a quarter of households in Kestermoor do not have a car, that buses reduce congestion and vehicle emissions on the city's main roads, and that cheaper travel helps people on low incomes reach jobs, education and health appointments. Older and disabled people already travel free under the national concessionary pass scheme.

Critics argue that much of the money goes to people who would have travelled by bus anyway, and that surveys show passengers value frequency and reliability more highly than lower fares. They say the £18 million would be better spent restoring routes that have been cut, especially in suburban and rural areas, where Ridgeway has warned that some services may be withdrawn.

Extract C: Franchising
The Combined Authority is consulting on bus franchising, a model already introduced in Greater Manchester. Under franchising, the authority would decide routes, timetables and fares, and would keep the fare revenue. Operators would bid in competitive tenders for contracts, typically lasting five to seven years, to run groups of routes, and would be paid a fee per vehicle-km operated, with bonuses or penalties linked to punctuality. The authority would buy the main depots so that any winning bidder could use them, and a single ticket would be valid on all buses.

Supporters say franchising would create an integrated network, allow profitable corridors to cross-subsidise socially valuable routes, and replace competition on the road with competition for the market. Critics point out that the authority would bear the risk if passenger numbers fall, that the transition is estimated to cost tens of millions of pounds, and that Ridgeway may be the only operator large enough to bid for most contracts.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge/Application: Franchising as a form of regulation: the public authority specifies the service and operators compete for the market through competitive tendering. Impact of intervention on prices, quality, efficiency, choice and profits; regulatory capture; government failure. Application: authority sets routes, fares and timetables and keeps the revenue; contracts of five to seven years paid per vehicle-km with punctuality incentives; authority buys depots; single ticket; transition costs of tens of millions; Ridgeway may be the only large bidder; Greater Manchester has already introduced franchising.
Analysis: Integrated ticketing removes the network-effect barrier, so passengers can change buses without paying twice, raising the value of the network and demand. Buying depots removes an essential-facility barrier, making tenders more contestable. Cross-subsidy allows profitable corridors to fund socially valuable routes (Table 2 shows rural and suburban routes make losses), addressing positive externalities and equity. Competition for the market can drive efficiency: bidders must offer low cost per vehicle-km to win, so X-inefficiency falls, and on-road predatory behaviour (Extract A) ends. Punctuality bonuses and penalties give incentives for quality. The authority can plan frequency, which passengers value most.
Evaluation: Few bidders: if Ridgeway is the only operator large enough, tenders are not competitive, so contract prices may be high (an effective monopoly at each tender) and the authority may be captured by its main supplier. Operators paid per vehicle-km no longer have an incentive to attract passengers, so service innovation may depend on the authority's ability (information gaps, government failure). Financial risk shifts to taxpayers if passenger numbers fall, and transition costs have an opportunity cost. Contracts of five to seven years reduce the ability to respond to change. Outcomes depend on contract design and monitoring. The alternative of enhanced partnerships or better-targeted subsidy could achieve some gains at lower cost. The Greater Manchester experience is recent, so evidence on long-run outcomes is limited. A justified conclusion should state which passengers are likely to gain (those making multi-leg trips, suburban and rural users) and the conditions required.
Levels: Knowledge, application and analysis (up to 9 marks)
Level 1 (1–3): Isolated knowledge, often limited to definitions; little or no use of the extracts or data; analysis is absent or a list of unconnected assertions.
Level 2 (4–6): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but are incomplete or one-sided; any diagram is partly accurate or not explained.
Level 3 (7–9): Precise knowledge fully integrated with the extracts and figures; developed, logical chains of reasoning for each point; accurate diagrams (where relevant) explained and used in the argument.
Levels: Evaluation (up to 6 marks)
Level 1 (1–2): Evaluation is generic or simply asserted, with no supporting reasoning.
Level 2 (3–4): Relevant evaluation with some supporting reasoning, but it is not developed across the answer or does not lead to a clear judgement.
Level 3 (5–6): Sustained evaluation that weighs the arguments, prioritises the most significant factors, uses the context or data, and reaches a fully justified judgement.
A* answer: Analyses how franchising changes contestability, network effects and cross-subsidy using evidence from all three extracts and Table 2, weighs these against risks of weak competition for contracts, regulatory capture and cost to taxpayers, and reaches a conditional judgement based on the number of credible bidders and the quality of contract design.

questions.prompt:
Answer EITHER (a) OR (b). Start your answer by writing (a) or (b).

(a) Many firms with monopoly power charge different prices to different groups of customers for the same product, for example peak and off-peak rail fares, airline seats sold at different times, and student discounts for software. Evaluate the view that price discrimination benefits consumers as well as producers.

(b) In the UK, healthcare and school education are mainly provided by the state free at the point of use, while most other goods and services are allocated by the price mechanism. Evaluate the view that free markets allocate scarce resources more efficiently than governments.
questions.mark_scheme:
This mark scheme covers both options. Mark the option the candidate chose using the indicative content below and the shared level descriptors. Mark split: Knowledge, application and analysis up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks.

OPTION (a): Price discrimination by firms with monopoly power
Knowledge/Application: Third-degree price discrimination: charging different prices to different groups of consumers for the same product, for reasons not related to cost. Conditions: price-setting power, ability to separate markets with different PEDs, and prevention of resale (market seepage). Profit maximisation where MC = MR in each sub-market, with a higher price in the more inelastic market. First-degree (perfect) discrimination converts all consumer surplus into producer surplus. Application: peak and off-peak rail fares (commuters with inelastic demand), airline yield management, student and educational software pricing, cinema concessions, pharmaceutical pricing across countries.
Analysis: Producers: higher total revenue and profit than a single price; consumer surplus transferred to producer surplus in the inelastic market. Consumers: those in the inelastic market (peak commuters) pay more and lose consumer surplus, while those in the elastic market (off-peak travellers, students) may pay less than under a single price and some are able to buy who otherwise would not. Output may rise, so allocative efficiency can improve compared with single-price monopoly, reducing deadweight loss; under perfect discrimination output reaches P = MC. Extra profit may fund investment and innovation (dynamic efficiency), or cross-subsidise services that would otherwise not be provided (rural rail routes, off-peak services). Spreading demand across time (peak pricing) uses capacity more efficiently, reducing congestion.
Evaluation: It depends on the type of discrimination: first-degree removes all consumer surplus, so consumers as a whole lose even though output rises. Effects on total output: if output does not increase, total welfare usually falls and the policy is mainly a transfer from consumers to producers. Equity: those charged more may be lower-income workers with inflexible hours, while discounts may go to groups who are not poor. Whether supernormal profit is reinvested depends on the firm's objectives and competitive pressure. Personalised pricing using data raises concerns about exploitation and information asymmetry, and may require regulation. In regulated industries (rail fares) the government limits the extent of discrimination. Judgement on who benefits overall, conditional on the type, output effect and use of profits.

OPTION (b): Free markets compared with government allocation
Knowledge/Application: The price mechanism: rationing, signalling and incentive functions; Adam Smith's invisible hand; Hayek's argument that prices convey dispersed information that central planners cannot gather; Marx's critique of free markets (inequality, exploitation). Allocative, productive and dynamic efficiency. Market failure: public goods, externalities, information gaps (for example in healthcare). Government failure: information gaps, distortion of price signals, unintended consequences, administrative costs. Application: NHS and state schools, free at the point of use; privatised utilities and their regulation; housing; examples of waiting lists as non-price rationing.
Analysis: Free markets: prices signal changes in scarcity and give profit incentives to switch resources to where consumers value them most, leading to allocative efficiency where P = MC in competitive markets; competition forces productive efficiency and drives innovation (dynamic efficiency); consumer sovereignty. Governments lack information and the profit motive, so state provision may suffer from X-inefficiency, excess demand rationed by queues, and poor responsiveness. However, markets fail: healthcare involves asymmetric information between patient and doctor and positive externalities (vaccination), and education is a merit good with external benefits, so the free market would under-consume. Monopoly power leads to allocative inefficiency. Market outcomes depend on the distribution of income, so allocation may be efficient but inequitable. State provision can achieve economies of scale (NHS as a monopsony buyer of medicines) and prevent over-consumption or under-consumption.
Evaluation: Efficiency must be distinguished from equity: free markets may be efficient for most private goods while state provision is justified for merit and public goods. Real-world markets are rarely perfectly competitive, and real governments are rarely fully informed, so the comparison is between imperfect markets and imperfect governments. The answer varies by good: food and clothing are efficiently allocated by markets, defence and street lighting require the state, and healthcare and education are mixed. Mixed approaches such as regulation, internal markets and contracting out may combine the strengths of both. Long-run versus short-run efficiency: markets may underinvest in long-term projects. A judgement should identify the conditions under which each allocates resources more efficiently.

Levels: Knowledge, application and analysis (up to 16 marks)
Level 1 (1–4): Some relevant knowledge, often in the form of definitions; little application to examples or the UK economy; analysis is descriptive or confused.
Level 2 (5–8): Accurate knowledge with some relevant application; one or two chains of reasoning that are partial or one-sided; diagrams present but not fully explained or partly inaccurate.
Level 3 (9–12): Accurate knowledge applied to realistic examples; several developed chains of reasoning with appropriate diagrams; some gaps in logic or balance.
Level 4 (13–16): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout to well-chosen examples; fully developed, logical chains of reasoning covering both sides; accurate diagrams integrated into the argument.
Levels: Evaluation (up to 9 marks)
Level 1 (1–3): Evaluation is generic or simply asserted, with no supporting reasoning.
Level 2 (4–6): Relevant evaluation with some supporting reasoning, but it is not developed across the answer or does not lead to a clear judgement.
Level 3 (7–9): Sustained evaluation that weighs the arguments, prioritises the most significant factors, uses the context or data, and reaches a fully justified judgement.
A* answer: Chooses one option and builds a focused, balanced argument with accurate diagrams (third-degree price discrimination with two sub-markets and MC = MR in each for (a); welfare loss from market failure set against the costs of government failure for (b)), applies precise real examples, and reaches a supported judgement that depends on clearly stated conditions (for example, whether output rises and how profits are used for (a); the type of good and the extent of information failure for (b)).
